title: The State of Front-End: Building Progressive Components
description: In the beginning, Tim Berners-Lee created HTML. Then Brendan Eich created JavaScript. And finally, Håkon Wium Lie created CSS. This was — and still is — the Holy Trinity of Front End-development. This
body_html:
In the beginning, Tim Berners-Lee created HTML.
Then Brendan Eich created JavaScript.
And finally, Håkon Wium Lie created CSS.

This was — and still is — the Holy Trinity of Front End-development.
This is how it worked then, and still works:

HTML = Content
CSS = Styling of content
JavaScript: Interaction with content

Because JavaScript lacked an easy way to select and add events to elements,  jQuery came along. For many years JavaScript became jQuery — many developers didn’t even know how to write JavaScript without jQuery, so JavaScript were nicknamed Vanilla JS, to make it sound like a framework (or so I guess).

But JavaScript evolved, surpassed jQuery, and the site You Might Not Need jQuery was launched to demonstrate this. It created an outcry back then, but many developers switched to Vanilla JS and didn’t look back.

Today we have loads and loads of JavaScript frameworks and they all have the same thing in common: They’re built with Vanilla JS.

For CSS, we can paint a similar picture: Today we can write/compile our CSS in SASS/SCSS, LESS, postCSS etc., but they all output the same thing: CSS (or maybe we should nickname it Vanilla CSS?).

All 3 languages have evolved tremendously during the years, but they’re all built with exactly the same structure/mindset as in 1989, 1995 and 1996 when the initial versions were launched.

About a month ago, a new site, You Might Not Need JavaScript, were launched.
Of course it created an outcry, and I can understand why:

How can you have interaction without JavaScript?

After all, that’s it’s role in the Holy Trinity!

Interaction can, in many cases, be simplified to this: state.
Is the element Selected? Unselected? Hovered? Focused?

So much logic, on any website, is based on adding or removing style-classes from an element based on state.

JavaScript does not have monopoly on setting state. In fact, HTML has always had state, it might just not be that obvious.

Any <input>-element has state. Whatever you do to an input will be preserved if you navigate away from the given page and then use your browser’s Back-button to go back to that page. Only a page-reload or JavaScript (or setting the value or autocomplete attributes) can change this default behaviour.

When a form is processed, you can almost feel the state/logic:

IF this is checked THEN do something AND IF radio-button-group is this OR that OR that THEN do something.

This same logic can, by the use of <input>-checkboxes and radio-buttons, be used for controlling state on not just forms, but other components as well. And — come to think of it — before CSS, that’s exactly how you would make users choose between various options on a webpage.

Styling state

With CSS3 it became possible to style the :checked-state of a radio-button or checkbox.
For reasons unknown, it became known as the checkbox hack, when it really should be called: Styling the :checked-state of a radio-button or checkbox (!)

In addition to styling the :checked-state, CSS3 can also style these states:

:active
:focus
:hover
:in-range
:invalid*
:out-of-range
:target
:valid*

*) In conjunction with :optional and :required, these selectors can dynamically indicate valid and invalid form-fields without JavaScript. All selectors can also be used in conjunction with the :not()-selector.

It’s important to notice, that the actual state is controlled by HTML, not CSS — CSS is only styling the state, so I have do disagree with Hugo Giraudel in this blog post (this is the first time I disagree with him, he’s a front-end-superstar!)

Benefits

What are the benefits of using HTML state?

  • Instant UI.
  • Preserves state.
  • Keyboard navigable. By default, radio-buttons in a radio-button-group can be selected with the arrow-keys and toggled with spacebar.
  • Progressive Enhancement.
    Make the component work without JavaScript for basic functionality and then add JavaScript for setting WAI-ARIA-states, JavaScript-based animations etc.
    If JavaScript fails/breaks (and this can be caused by loading external scripts you don’t control), the component will still work. Also, for users in third-world countries with slower devices running Opera Mini (according to Bruce Lawson, that’s a lot of users), JavaScript will be “cut off” after 5 seconds, so if your components are dependant on large JavaScript-frameworks, they might not work for these users.
  • Works in emails. Sort of … Google has just removed support for all CSS pseudo-selector-states except :hover in Gmail, but I suspect it will come back. I don’t have the current statistics, but the :checked-state used to work in more than 80% of email-clients. Take a look at Litmus.com for more info on interactive emails.

Example: Accordion

A couple of years ago, I was asked to do an accordion-component with the following specs:

  • The accordion should toggle, meaning any selection would auto-collapse, when another was chosen.
  • Selections within the expanded content should toggle, but here, multiple selections were allowed.
  • All selections should be keyboard-navigable.
  • All states should be preserved upon navigation, meaning, that if you navigated away from the page and went back, everything should be “folded out” as when you left the page.

Naturally, this required a lot of JavaScript and DOM-iterations for each selection (add “selected” class from active element, remove it from the others), keyboard-event listener, saving state to a cookie (or localStorage) etc. etc.

By using radio-buttons for the auto-collapse and checkboxes for the multiple selections, no JavaScript was necessary. Keyboard-navigation and remembering state upon navigation were thrown in for free.

Even Apple does it …

On Apples’s new website, checkboxes are used multiple places to toggle state.

Upcoming

In an upcoming post, I will demonstrate a true progressive component with state controlled by HTML, styled by CSS – and with JavaScript for adding WAI-ARIA-states.

Happy coding!
